## Basic RMarkdown

### What is a YAML header?

This is the YAML Header. Notice it is enclosed in "---" it is used to store information. This needs to be at the very top of the Rmd document.

### It includes metadata like the following:

````{verbatim}
---
title: Lab 2
author: Mona Xue
date: 2026-01-23
---

````


### Markdown

````{verbatim}

# This is a heading. Notice the "#" and space afterward

# This is a sub-heading. Notice the "#" and space afterward

Markdown is a markup language that makes formatting text easier.

It allows you to write normal text alongside code.

````

````{=html}

<br></br>

<h3> This is a heading. Notice the "#" and space afterward </h3>

<h4> This is a sub-heading. Notice the "#" and space afterward </h4>

<p>Markdown is a markup language that makes formatting text easier.</p>

<p>It allows you to write normal text alongside code.</p>

````



### R Code Chunk

````{verbatim}
```{r}

# This is your R code chunk.
# This is where you write R code.

```
````

Inside code blocks, you denote comments with #. Note: outside of a code block, these become headings.

````{verbatim}
```{r}
# This is a comment. 

```
````

### With both Markdown and R code = RMarkdown

:::: {.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}

````{verbatim}
# This is a heading

You can write text like this

```{r}
# This is a comment
a <- 1
b <- 2

a
```
````

## Basic Syntax

### Variables

This is how you assign values to a variable
```{r}

a <- 1 

```

### Vectors

This is how you create a vector. You use the notation `c()`
```{r}
x <- c(a, "a")
y <- c(1, 2, 3)
z <- 1:3 # This is the same as y. The : indicates a vector from 1 to 3
```

To print the variable, simply run the name of the variable
```{r}
x
```

Notice that without quotes, `a` refers to a variable and prints the number assigned to it (1), whereas with quotes, `"a"` prints out just the letter. When things are wrapped with quotes, they are called ***strings***.

To choose a specific element of a vector, you can use `[]`
```{r}
x[2]
y[3]
y[c(2, 3)]
y[1:2]

```

### Vector examples
```{r}
a <- 1 # assigns the number 1 to the variable `a`
b <- 1:3 # creates a list of numbers from 1 to 3 and assigns it to `b`
c <- c(3,4,5) # creates a list that includes 3, 4, 5 and assigns it to `c`
c[4] <- 6 # assigns the 4th element of `c` to the number 6, resulting in the list 3, 4, 5, 6
d <- c(b,c) # combines the lists b and c, producing the list 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6, and assigns this to `d`
```


## Doing math

```{r}
1 + 1
```

### Adding a single number to a vector

```{r}
y + 1 # Adds the single number to all elements in the vector
```

### Adding a vector to a vector
```{r}
y + z # Adds the 1st to the 1st, the 2nd to the 2nd, etc.

```


### Other useful functions

```r
sum(y) # Adds together the elements of y

mean(y) # Takes the mean of the elements of y

2 * 2 # Multiplication

2 / 2 # Division

2^2 # To the power of 2

sqrt(2) # Square root of 2

(2 + 2) * 2 / (2) # Order of operations still apply, remember to use parentheses when you need to


```


## Adv. Rmd formatting {#adv-format}

### 1. Remove unwanted warnings and messages

To remove unwanted warnings and messages from the output, use these at the very top of a code block. For instance, the following removes the warning messages from loading packages.

````{verbatim}
```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

data <- read_csv("heights.csv")

```
````

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: false

library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

data <- read_csv("./data/heights.csv")

```

### 2. Print nicer dataframes and tables

Use `knitr::kable()` to print nicer dataframes and tables


```{r}
knitr::kable(head(data))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
summary_table <- data %>% group_by(sex) %>% summarize(SampleSize=n(),Mean=mean(heights), SD=sd(heights),SE=SD/sqrt(SampleSize))
```

```{r}
knitr::kable(summary_table)
```

### 3. Round values to fewer decimals

Use `round()` to round to fewer decimals. For example, the following rounds the variables `a` to two decimal places.

```r
round(a, 2)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

CIs <- summary_table %>% mutate(CIs = paste0("[", round(Mean-1.96*SE,2), ", ", round(Mean+1.96*SE,2), "]")) %>% select(sex, CIs)

```

### 4. Create outputs like `r CIs[1,2]`

Use `paste0()` to add together strings and variables. This is useful for reporting CIs. For instance,

```r
CIs <- CIs %>% mutate(CIs = paste0("[", round(LowerCI,2), ", ", round(UpperCI,2), "]")) %>% select(group, CIs)
knitr::kable(CIs)
```
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| 
knitr::kable(CIs)
```

### 5. Reference variables from r code directly in your paragraphs

Use ``` `r ` ``` to use r code in your paragraphs so you can reference variables from you code chunks. For example:

```{verbatim}
The the CIs for groups one and two are `r CIs[1,2]` and `r CIs[2,2]`, respectively.
```

The the CIs for groups one and two are `r CIs[1,2]` and `r CIs[2,2]`, respectively.

Note that [1,2] stands for row 1 and column 2 of the CI table, and [2,2] stands for row 2 and column 2 of the CI table.
